title: Mark, looking back
hookLine: the breathless gospel that ended in trembling
tomorrow: two houses, same street, same sermon. why does one fall?

cards: Very early on the first day of the week, three women walk to a tomb carrying spices: Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome. All the way there they've been asking each other who will roll the stone away.

When they look up, it's already rolled back. Inside, on the right, sits a young man in a long white garment. What he tells them sends them running out into the morning, shaking, and saying nothing to anyone.

teach.b: Here's what the young man said: “But go your way, tell his disciples and Peter that he goeth before you into Galilee: there shall ye see him, as he said unto you.”
And Peter, the one who had denied him, is named on purpose.

Then the line readers keep coming back to: “And they went out quickly, and fled from the sepulchre; for they trembled and were amazed: neither said they any thing to any man; for they were afraid.” Why end a gospel there?
Some readers hear the book stop right at that verse; others read on into the verses printed after it. Either way, verse eight is worth sitting with. Mark doesn't do slow.
No birth story, no family tree, and one word piling up: straightway. Straightway out of the water, straightway they left their nets.

And here's the detail to tell a friend: his first verse is a title, “The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God.” The beginning. So some readers hear the trembling ending as a door back to the start.
He goeth before you into Galilee: back where it all began, by the lake and the nets, out in ordinary life.
Jesus isn't waiting at the tomb. He's already ahead. Mark gives fear an honest place on Easter morning, and the promise still stands.

how: Christians read Mark's Gospel in worship and at home; some read it straight through in one sitting, and some linger over its sudden ending at 16:8.

games.q: your friend got frightening news about her dad and hasn't told anyone, because she can't find words. what does Mark's ending suggest?
o: her silence means she's failing; she has to speak today.
fear and silence can be part of the story; the promise stands, and words can come later.
she should keep it to herself for good; some news is never shared.
games.why: Mark ends with trembling women who said nothing, for they were afraid, and the promise was still true: he goeth before you.

practice: Say the young man's words out loud, slowly: he goeth before you. Then sit with the last line, for they were afraid, and let both be true at once. If you pray, bring one fear of your own and set the promise down beside it.

wordCard.voice: Mark. The breathless Gospel that begins with a title and ends with trembling women and a promise: he goes ahead.

orig.note: the Greek for 'goeth before' in Mark 16:7: he leads the way ahead.

carryVoice: Your line: he goes before you. Afraid and promised, both on the same morning. Until tomorrow.
